title: Two-tailed one-sample Z-test for bottling volume
scenario_markdown: A beverage bottling plant operates an automated filling line calibrated to fill containers to a target mean volume of $\mu = 2.00\text{ liters}$. Long-term engineering data confirms that the process standard deviation is known to be $\sigma = 0.05\text{ liters}$. A quality audit samples $n = 36$ bottles from the morning production shift and measures a sample mean of $\bar{x} = 2.02\text{ liters}$. Conduct a two-tailed hypothesis test at significance level $\alpha = 0.05$ to test whether the line is operating out of calibration ($H_0: \mu = 2.00$ vs $H_1: \mu \ne 2.00$).
assumptions: Bottling volumes are approximately normally distributed, and CLT applies since n = 36 >= 30
The process standard deviation is known (sigma = 0.05 L), justifying the standard normal Z test
Independent random sample of filled bottles from the production run

approval.notes: Reviewed derivation: null_mu = 2.00, x_bar = 2.02, sigma = 0.05, n = 36. SE = 0.05 / 6 = 0.0083333. Z = (2.02 - 2.00) / 0.0083333 = 2.40. One-tailed tail prob = 0.0081975. Two-tailed p-value = 2 * 0.0081975 = 0.016395 (approx 0.0164). Since p-val < 0.05 and |Z| = 2.40 > 1.960, reject H0. Excel: =2*(1 - NORM.S.DIST(2.40, TRUE)).

stages.prompt_markdown: Calculate the standard error of the mean $SE$ and the standardized test statistic $Z = \frac{\bar{x} - \mu_0}{\sigma / \sqrt{n}}$.

options.hint_markdown: Standard error divides $\sigma$ by $\sqrt{n} = \sqrt{36} = 6$, giving $0.05/6 \approx 0.00833\text{ L}$.
The numerator is $\bar{x} - \mu_0 = 2.02 - 2.00 = +0.02$, which is positive.

stages.explanation_markdown: The standard error is $SE = \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}} = \frac{0.05}{\sqrt{36}} = \frac{0.05}{6} \approx 0.008333\text{ L}$. The test statistic standardizes the difference between the observed sample mean $\bar{x} = 2.02$ and hypothesized mean $\mu_0 = 2.00$: $Z = \frac{2.02 - 2.00}{0.0083333} = \frac{0.02}{0.0083333} = +2.40$. The sample mean lies $2.40$ standard errors above the target calibration.

stages.prompt_markdown: Compute the two-tailed $p$-value for this test statistic $Z = +2.40$.

options.hint_markdown: Because the test is two-tailed ($H_1: \mu \ne 2.00$), the one-tailed probability must be doubled to account for deviations in either direction.
$0.9918$ is the area below $Z = 2.40$. Tail area is $1 - 0.9918 = 0.0082$, doubled for two tails.

stages.explanation_markdown: For a two-tailed test, the $p$-value measures the probability of observing a test statistic at least as extreme as $|Z| = 2.40$ in either tail: $p\text{-value} = 2 \times P(Z \ge 2.40) = 2 \times [1 - \Phi(2.40)] = 2 \times (1 - 0.99180) = 2 \times 0.00820 = 0.0164$ (or $1.64\%$). In Excel: `=2*(1 - NORM.S.DIST(2.40, TRUE))`.

stages.prompt_markdown: What is the statistical decision at $\alpha = 0.05$ and the appropriate conclusion regarding the bottling line?

options.text_markdown: Reject $H_0$ because $p\text{-value} = 0.0164 < 0.05$ (and $|Z| = 2.40 > 1.960$). There is statistically significant evidence that the bottling line is out of calibration.
Fail to reject $H_0$ because $\bar{x} = 2.02$ is only $0.02\text{ L}$ above $2.00$, which is practically negligible.
options.hint_markdown: Statistical decision rules are strictly defined by comparing the p-value to alpha ($p < \alpha$), which dictates rejecting $H_0$ here.
The test significance level was set at $\alpha = 0.05$, not $0.01$. Furthermore, classical testing never 'accepts' $H_0$.

stages.explanation_markdown: Because the $p$-value ($0.0164$) is less than the significance level $\alpha = 0.05$ (or equivalently, test statistic $|Z| = 2.40$ exceeds the critical value $Z^* = 1.960$), we reject $H_0$. There is statistically significant evidence at the $5\%$ level to conclude that the filling machine mean volume differs from $2.00\text{ liters}$, requiring engineering recalibration.
